entries.5496cd1ec2f69abe5193fb40287ec50468b8f6f5: <div sID="gen7598" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="2Kgs.25" sID="2Kgs.25"/> <div eID="gen7598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7599" type="x-p"/> Ever since David's time Jerusalem had been a celebrated place, beautiful for situation and the joy of the whole earth: while the book of psalms lasts that name will sound great. In the New Testament we read much of it, when it was, as here, ripening again for its ruin. In the close of the Bible we read of a new Jerusalem. Every thing therefore that concerns Jerusalem is worthy our regard. In this chapter we have, I. The utter destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, the city besieged and taken (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1-2Kgs.25.4">ver. 1-4</reference>), the houses burnt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.8-2Kgs.25.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>), and wall broken down (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.10">ver. 10</reference>), and the inhabitants carried away into captivity, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.11-2Kgs.25.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. The glory of Jerusalem was, 1. That it was the royal city, where were set "the thrones of the house of David;" but that glory has now departed, for the prince is made a most miserable prisoner, the seed royal is destroyed (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.5-2Kgs.25.7">ver. 5-7</reference>), and the principal officers are put to death, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18-2Kgs.25.21">ver. 18-21</reference>. 2. That it was the holy city, where was the testimony of Israel; but that glory has departed, for Solomon's temple is burnt to the ground (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.9">ver. 9</reference>) and the sacred vessels that remained are carried away to Babylon, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.13-2Kgs.25.17">ver. 13-17</reference>. Thus has Jerusalem become as a widow, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.1">Lam. i. 1</reference>. Ichabod—Where is the glory? II. The distraction and dispersion of the remnant that was left in Judah under Gedaliah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.22-2Kgs.25.26">ver. 22-26</reference>. III. The countenance which, after thirty-seven years' imprisonment, was given to Jehoiachin the captive king of Judah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.27-2Kgs.25.30">ver. 27-30</reference>.
entries.38b772934c8eadcf0e9184d318350e67ac0b06c5: <div eID="gen7599" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jerusalem Besieged. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 590.)</title> <div sID="gen7600" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he, and all his host, against Jerusalem, and pitched against it; and they built forts against it round about. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the city was besieged unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah. <hi type="super">3</hi> And on the ninth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the <hi type="italic">fourth</hi> month the famine prevailed in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the city was broken up, and all the men of war <hi type="italic">fled</hi> by night by the way of the gate between two walls, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the king's garden: (now the Chaldees <hi type="italic">were</hi> against the city round about:) and <hi type="italic">the king</hi> went the way toward the plain. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the army of the Chaldees pursued after the king, and overtook him in the plains of Jericho: and all his army were scattered from him. <hi type="super">6</hi> So they took the king, and brought him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah; and they gave judgment upon him. <hi type="super">7</hi> And they slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him with fetters of brass, and carried him to Babylon. <div eID="gen7600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7601" type="x-p"/> We left king Zedekiah in rebellion against the king of Babylon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.20">ch. xxiv. 20</reference>), contriving and endeavouring to shake off his yoke, when he was no way able to do it, nor took the right method by making God his friend first. Now here we have an account of the fatal consequences of that attempt. <div eID="gen7601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7602" type="x-p"/> I. The king of Babylon's army laid siege to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1">v. 1</reference>. What should hinder them when the country was already in their possession? <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.2">ch. xxiv. 2</reference>. They <hi type="italic">built forts against the city round about,</hi> whence, by such arts of war as they then had, they battered it, sent into it instruments of death, and kept out of it the necessary supports of life. Formerly Jerusalem had been compassed with the favour of God as with a shield, but now their defence had departed from them and their enemies surrounded them on every side. Those that by sin have provoked God to leave them will find that <hi type="italic">innumerable evils will compass them about.</hi> Two years this siege lasted; at first the army retired, for fear of the king of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.11">Jer. xxxvii. 11</reference>), but, finding him not so powerful as they thought, they soon returned, with a resolution not to quit the city till they had made themselves masters of it. <div eID="gen7602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7603" type="x-p"/> II. During this siege the famine prevailed (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.3">v. 3</reference>), so that for a long time they <hi type="italic">ate their bread by weight and with care,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.16">Ezek. iv. 16</reference>. Thus they were punished for their gluttony and excess, their <hi type="italic">fulness of bread</hi> and <hi type="italic">feeding themselves without fear.</hi> At length <hi type="italic">there was no bread for the people of the land,</hi> that is, the common people, the soldiers, whereby they were weakened and rendered unfit for service. Now they ate their own children for want of food. See this foretold by one prophet (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">Ezek. v. 10</reference>) and bewailed by another, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.3-Lam.4.12">Lam. iv. 3</reference>, &c. Jeremiah earnestly persuaded the king to surrender (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.17">Jer. xxxviii. 17</reference>), but his heart was hardened to his destruction. <div eID="gen7603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7604" type="x-p"/> III. At length the city was taken by storm: it was <hi type="italic">broken up,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.4">v. 4</reference>. The besiegers made a breach in the wall, at which they forced their way into it. The besieged, unable any longer to defend it, endeavoured to quit it, and make the best of their way; and many, no doubt, were put to the sword, the victorious army being much exasperated by their obstinacy. <div eID="gen7604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7605" type="x-p"/> IV. The king, his family, and all his great men, made their escape in the night, by some secret passages which the besiegers either had not discovered or did not keep their eye upon, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.4">v. 4</reference>. But those as much deceive themselves who think to escape God's judgments as those who think to brave them; the feet of him that flees from them will as surely fail as the hands of him that fights against them. When God judges he will overcome. Intelligence was given to the Chaldeans of the king's flight, and which way he had gone, so that they soon overtook him, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.5">v. 5</reference>. His guards were scattered from him, every man shifting for his own safety. Had he put himself under God's protection, that would not have failed him now. He presently fell into the enemies' hands, and here we are told what they did with him. 1. He was brought to the king of Babylon, and tried by a council of war for rebelling against him who set him up, and to whom he had sworn fidelity. God and man had a quarrel with him for this; see <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.16-Ezek.17.21">Ezek. xvii. 16</reference>, &c. The king of Babylon now lay at Riblah (which lay between Judea and Babylon), that he might be ready to give orders both to his court at home and his army abroad. 2. His <hi type="italic">sons were slain before his eyes,</hi> though children, that this doleful spectacle, the last his eyes were to behold, might leave an impression of grief and horror upon his spirit as long as he lived. In slaying his sons, they showed their indignation at his falsehood, and in effect declared that neither he nor any of his were fit to be trusted, and therefore that they were not fit to live. 3. His eyes were put out, by which he was deprived of that common comfort of human life which is given even to <hi type="italic">those that are in misery, and to the bitter in soul,</hi> the light of the sun, by which he was also disabled for any service. He dreaded being mocked, and therefore would not be persuaded to yield (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.19">Jer. xxxviii. 19</reference>), but that which he feared came upon him with a witness, and no doubt added much to his misery; for, as those that are deaf suspect that every body talks of them, so those that are blind suspect that every body laughs at them. By this two prophecies that seemed to contradict one another were both fulfilled. Jeremiah prophesied that Zedekiah should be brought to Babylon, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.5">Jer. xxxii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.3">xxxiv. 3</reference>. Ezekiel prophesied that he should not see Babylon, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Ezek. xii. 13</reference>. He was brought thither, but, his eyes being put out, he did not see it. Thus he ended his days, before he ended his life. 4. He was <hi type="italic">bound in fetters of brass</hi> and so <hi type="italic">carried to Babylon.</hi> He that was blind needed not be bound (his blindness fettered him), but, for his greater disgrace, they led him bound; only, whereas common malefactors are laid in irons (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.18">Ps. cv. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.10">cvii. 10</reference>), he, being a prince, was bound with fetters of brass; but that the metal was somewhat nobler and lighter was little comfort, while still he was in fetters. Let it not seem strange if those that have been held in the cords of iniquity come to be thus <hi type="italic">held in the cords of affliction,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.8">Job xxxvi. 8</reference>.
entries.1d27c80f1977c7038e0e4820cd91bc514442c64a: <div eID="gen7605" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Temple Destroyed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen7606" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And in the fifth month, on the seventh <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, unto Jerusalem: <hi type="super">9</hi> And he burnt the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great <hi type="italic">man's</hi> house burnt he with fire. <hi type="super">10</hi> And all the army of the Chaldees, that <hi type="italic">were with</hi> the captain of the guard, brake down the walls of Jerusalem round about. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now the rest of the people <hi type="italic">that were</hi> left in the city, and the fugitives that fell away to the king of Babylon, with the remnant of the multitude, did Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carry away. <hi type="super">12</hi> But the captain of the guard left of the poor of the land <hi type="italic">to be</hi> vinedressers and husbandmen. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the pillars of brass that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the bases, and the brasen sea that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , did the Chaldees break in pieces, and carried the brass of them to Babylon. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the pots, and the shovels, and the snuffers, and the spoons, and all the vessels of brass wherewith they ministered, took they away. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the firepans, and the bowls, <hi type="italic">and</hi> such things as <hi type="italic">were</hi> of gold, <hi type="italic">in</hi> gold, and of silver, <hi type="italic">in</hi> silver, the captain of the guard took away. <hi type="super">16</hi> The two pillars, one sea, and the bases which Solomon had made for the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; the brass of all these vessels was without weight. <hi type="super">17</hi> The height of the one pillar <hi type="italic">was</hi> eighteen cubits, and the chapiter upon it <hi type="italic">was</hi> brass: and the height of the chapiter three cubits; and the wreathen work, and pomegranates upon the chapiter round about, all of brass: and like unto these had the second pillar with wreathen work. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the door: <hi type="super">19</hi> And out of the city he took an officer that was set over the men of war, and five men of them that were in the king's presence, which were found in the city, and the principal scribe of the host, which mustered the people of the land, and threescore men of the people of the land <hi type="italic">that were</hi> found in the city: <hi type="super">20</hi> And Nebuzar-adan captain of the guard took these, and brought them to the king of Babylon to Riblah: <hi type="super">21</hi> And the king of Babylon smote them, and slew them at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was carried away out of their land. <div eID="gen7606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7607" type="x-p"/> Though we have reason to think that the army of the Chaldeans were much enraged against the city for holding out with so much stubbornness, yet they did not therefore put all to fire and sword as soon as they had taken the city (which is too commonly done in such cases), but about a month after (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.8 2Kgs.25.3">v. 8 with v. 3</reference>) Nebuzar-adan was sent with orders to complete the destruction of Jerusalem. This space God gave them to repent, after all the foregoing days of his patience, but in vain; their hearts (for aught that appears) were still hardened, and therefore execution is awarded to the utmost. 1. The city and temple are burnt, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.9">v. 9</reference>. It does not appear that the king of Babylon designed to send any colonies to people Jerusalem and therefore he ordered it to be laid in ashes, as a nest of rebels. At the burning of the king's house and <hi type="italic">the houses of the great men</hi> one cannot so much wonder (the inhabitants had, by their sins, made them combustible), but that the <hi type="italic">house of the Lord</hi> should perish in these flames, that that holy and beautiful house should be burnt with fire (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.11">Isa. lxiv. 11</reference>), is very strange. That house which David prepared for, and which Solomon built at such a vast expense—that house which had the eye and heart of God perpetually upon it (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.3">1 Kings ix. 3</reference>)—might not that have been snatched as a brand out of this burning? No, it must not be fire-proof against God's judgments. This stately structure must be turned into ashes, and it is probable the ark in it, for the enemies, having heard how dearly the Philistines paid for the abusing of it, durst not seize that, nor did any of its friends take care to preserve it, for then we should have heard of it again in the second temple. One of the apocryphal writers does indeed tell us that the prophet Jeremiah got it out of the temple, and conveyed it to a cave in Mount Nebo on the other side Jordan, and hid it there (<reference osisRef="2Macc.2.4-2Macc.2.5">2 Macc. ii. 4, 5</reference>), but that could not be, for Jeremiah was a close prisoner at that time. By the burning of the temple God would show how little cares for the external pomp of his worship when the life and power of religion are neglected. The people trusted to the temple, as if that would protect them in their sins (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jer. vii. 4</reference>), but God, by this, let them know that when they had profaned it they would find it but a refuge of lies. This temple had stood about 420, some say 430 years. The people having forfeited the promises made concerning it, those promises must be understood of the gospel-temple, which is God's rest for ever. It is observable that the second temple was burnt by the Romans the same month, and the same day of the month, that the first temple was burnt by the Chaldeans, which, Josephus says, was the tenth of August. 2. The walls of Jerusalem are demolished (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.10">v. 10</reference>), as if the victorious army would be revenged on them for having kept them out so long, or at least prevent the like opposition another time. Sin unwalls a people and takes away their defence. These walls were never repaired till Nehemiah's time. 3. The residue of the people are carried away captive to Babylon, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.11">v. 11</reference>. Most of the inhabitants had perished by sword or famine, or had made their escape when the king did (for it is said, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.5">v. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">His army was scattered from him</hi>), so that there were very few left, who with the deserters, making in all but 832 persons (as appears, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.29">Jer. lii. 29</reference>), were carried away into captivity; only <hi type="italic">the poor of the land were left behind</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.12">v. 12</reference>), to till the ground and dress the vineyards for the Chaldeans. Sometimes poverty is a protection; for those that have nothing have nothing to lose. When the rich Jews, who had been oppressive to the poor, were made strangers, nay, prisoners, in an enemy's country, the poor whom they had despised and oppressed had liberty and peace in their own country. Thus Providence sometimes remarkably humbles the proud and favours those of low degree. 4. The brazen vessels, and other appurtenances of the temple, are carried away, those of silver and gold being most of them gone before. Those two famous columns of brass, <hi type="italic">Jachin</hi> and <hi type="italic">Boaz,</hi> which signified the strength and stability of the house of God, were broken to pieces and the brass of them was carried to Babylon, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.13">v. 13</reference>. When the things signified were sinned away what should the signs stand there for? Ahaz had profanely <hi type="italic">cut off the borders of the bases,</hi> and put <hi type="italic">the brazen sea upon a pavement of stones</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.17">2 Kings xvi. 17</reference>); justly therefore are the brass themselves, and the brazen sea, delivered into the enemy's hand. It is just with God to take away his ordinances from those that profane and abuse them, that curtail and depress them. Some things remained of gold and silver (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.15">v. 15</reference>) which were now carried off; but most of this plunder was brass, such a vast quantity of it that it is said to be <hi type="italic">without weight,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.16">v. 16</reference>. The carrying away of <hi type="italic">the vessels wherewith they ministered</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.14">v. 14</reference>) put an end to the ministration. It was a righteous thing with God to deprive those of the benefit of his worship who had slighted it so long and preferred false worships before it. Those that would have many altars shall now have none. 5. Several of the great men are slain in cold blood—Seraiah the chief priest (who was the father of Ezra as appears, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.1">Ezra vii. 1</reference>), the second priest (who, when there was occasion, officiated for him), and three door-keepers of the temple (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18">v. 18</reference>), the general of the army, five privy-counsellors (afterwards they made them up seven, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.25">Jer. lii. 25</reference>), the secretary of war, or pay-master of the army, and sixty country gentlemen who had concealed themselves in the city. These, being persons of some rank, were brought to the king of Babylon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.19-2Kgs.25.20">v. 19, 20</reference>), who ordered them to be all put to death (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.21">v. 21</reference>), when, in reason, they might have hoped that surely the bitterness of death was past. These the king of Babylon's revenge looked upon as most active in opposing him; but divine justice, we may suppose, looked upon them as ringleaders in that idolatry and impiety which were punished by these desolations. This completed the calamity: <hi type="italic">So Judah was carried away out of their land,</hi> about 860 years after they were put in possession of it by Joshua. Now the scripture was fulfilled, <hi type="italic">The Lord shall bring thee, and the king which thou shalt set over thee, into a nation which thou hast not known,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.28.36">Deut. xxviii. 36</reference>. Sin kept their fathers forty years out of Canaan, and now turned <hi type="italic">them</hi> out. The Lord is known by those judgments which he executes, and makes good that word which he has spoken, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amos iii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">You only have I known of all the families of the earth, therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.</hi>
entries.09af19f3976765289a187ab8a27b44176e65723e: <div eID="gen7607" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Dispersion of the Remnant of Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 552.)</title> <div sID="gen7608" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And <hi type="italic">as for</hi> the people that remained in the land of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left, even over them he made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, ruler. <hi type="super">23</hi> And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, there came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Careah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men. <hi type="super">24</hi> And Gedaliah sware to them, and to their men, and said unto them, Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you. <hi type="super">25</hi> But it came to pass in the seventh month, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the seed royal, came, and ten men with him, and smote Gedaliah, that he died, and the Jews and the Chaldees that were with him at Mizpah. <hi type="super">26</hi> And all the people, both small and great, and the captains of the armies, arose, and came to Egypt: for they were afraid of the Chaldees. <hi type="super">27</hi> And it came to pass in the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the seven and twentieth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Evil-merodach king of Babylon in the year that he began to reign did lift up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison; <hi type="super">28</hi> And he spake kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him in Babylon; <hi type="super">29</hi> And changed his prison garments: and he did eat bread continually before him all the days of his life. <hi type="super">30</hi> And his allowance <hi type="italic">was</hi> a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life. <div eID="gen7608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7609" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen7609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7610" type="x-p"/> I. The dispersion of the remaining people. The city of Jerusalem was quite laid waste. Some people there were in the land of Judah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.22">v. 22</reference>) that had weathered the storm, and (which was no small favour at this time, <reference osisRef="Jer.45.5">Jer. xlv. 5</reference>) had <hi type="italic">their lives given them for a prey.</hi> Now see, 1. What a good posture they were put into. The king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah, one of themselves, to be their governor and protector under him, a very good man, and one that would make the best of the bad, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.22">v. 22</reference>. His father Ahikam was one that countenanced and protected Jeremiah when the princes had vowed his death, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.24">Jer. xxvi. 24</reference>. It is probable that this Gedaliah, by the advice of Jeremiah, had gone over the Chaldeans, and had conducted himself so well that the king of Babylon entrusted him with the government. He resided not at Jerusalem, but at Mizpah, in the land of Benjamin, a place famous in Samuel's time. Thither those came who had fled from Zedekiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.4">v. 4</reference>) and put themselves under his protection (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.23">v. 23</reference>), which he assured them of if they would be patient and peaceable under the government of the king of Babylon, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.24">v. 24</reference>. Gedaliah, though he had not the pomp and power of a sovereign prince, yet might have been a greater blessing to them than many of their kings had been, especially having such a privy-council as Jeremiah, who was now with them, and interested himself in their affairs, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.5-Jer.40.6">Jer. xl. 5, 6</reference>. 2. What a fatal breach was made upon them, soon afterwards, by the death of Gedaliah, within two months after he entered upon his government. The utter extirpation of the Jews, for the present, was determined, and therefore it was in vain for them to think of taking root again: the whole land must be plucked up, <reference osisRef="Jer.45.4">Jer. xlv. 4</reference>. Yet this hopeful settlement is dashed to pieces, not by the Chaldeans, but by some of themselves. The things of their peace were so hidden from their eyes that they knew not when they were well off, nor would believe when they were told. (1.) They had a good governor of their own, and him they slew, out of spite to the Chaldeans, because he was appointed by Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.25">v. 25</reference>. Ishmael, who was of the royal family, envying Gedaliah's advancement and the happy settlement of the people under him, though he could not propose to set up himself, resolved to ruin him, and basely slew him and all his friends, both Jews and Chaldeans. Nebuchadnezzar would not, could not, have been a more mischievous enemy to their peace than this degenerate branch of the house of David was. (2.) They were as yet in their own good land, but they forsook it, and went to Egypt, for fear of the Chaldeans, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.26">v. 26</reference>. The Chaldeans had reason enough to be offended at the murder of Gedaliah; but if those that remained had humbly remonstrated, alleging that it was only the act of Ishmael and his party, we may suppose that those who were innocent of it, nay, who suffered greatly by it, would not have been punished for it: but, under pretence of this apprehension, contrary to the counsel of Jeremiah, they all went to Egypt, where, it is probable, they mixed with the Egyptians by degrees, and were never heard of more as Israelites. Thus was there a full end made of them by their own folly and disobedience, and Egypt had the last of them, that the last verse of that chapter of threatenings might be fulfilled, after all the rest, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.68">Deut. xxviii. 68</reference>, <hi type="italic">The Lord shall bring thee into Egypt again.</hi> These events are more largely related by the prophet Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.1-Jer.45.5">ch. xl. to ch. xlv.</reference> <hi type="italic">Quaeque ipse miserrima vidit, et quorum pars magna fuit—Which scenes he was doomed to behold, and in which he bore a melancholy part.</hi> <div eID="gen7610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7611" type="x-p"/> II. The reviving of the captive prince. Of Zedekiah we hear no more after he was carried blind to Babylon; it is probable that he did not live long, but that when he died he was buried with some marks of honour, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.5">Jer. xxxiv. 5</reference>. Of Jehoiachin, or Jeconiah, who surrendered himself (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12">ch. xxiv. 12</reference>), we are here told that as soon as Evil-merodach came to the crown, upon the death of his father Nebuchadnezzar, he released him out of prison (where he had lain thirty-seven years, and was now fifty-five years old), <hi type="italic">spoke kindly to him,</hi> paid more respect to him than to any other of the kings his father had left in captivity (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.28">v. 28</reference>), gave him princely clothing instead of his prison-garments, maintained him in his own palace (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.29">v. 29</reference>), and allowed him a pension for himself and his family in some measure corresponding to his rank, <hi type="italic">a daily rate for every day as long as he lived.</hi> Consider this, 1. As a very happy change of Jehoiachin's condition. To have honour and liberty after he had been so long in confinement and disgrace, the plenty and pleasure of a court after he had been so long accustomed to the straits and miseries of a prison, was like the return of the morning after a very dark and tedious night. Let none say that they shall never see good again because they have long seen little but evil; the most miserable know not what blessed turn Providence may yet give to their affairs, nor what comforts they are reserved for, <hi type="italic">according to the days wherein they have been afflicted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.15">Ps. cx. 15</reference>. However the death of afflicted saints is to them such a change as this was to Jehoiachin: it will release them out of their prison, shake off the body, that prison-garment, and open the way to their advancement; it will send them to the throne, to the table, of the King of kings, the glorious liberty of God's children. 2. As a very generous act of Evil-merodach's. He thought his father made the yoke of his captives too heavy, and therefore, with the tenderness of a man and the honour of a prince, made it lighter. It should seem all the kings he had in his power were favoured, but Jehoiachin above them all, some think for the sake of the antiquity of his family and the honour of his renowned ancestors, David and Solomon. None of the kings of the nations, it is likely, had descended from so long a race of kings in a direct lineal succession, and by a male line, as the king of Judah. The Jews say that this Evil-merodach had been himself imprisoned by his own father, when he returned from his madness, for some mismanagement at that time, and that in prison he contracted a friendship with Jehoiachin, in consequence of which, as soon as he had it in his power, he showed him this kindness as a sufferer, as a fellow-sufferer. Some suggest that Evil-merodach had learned from Daniel and his fellows the principles of the true religion, and was well affected to them, and upon that account favoured Jehoiachin. 3. As a kind dispensation of Providence, for the encouragement of the Jews in captivity, and the support of their faith and hope concerning their enlargement in due time. This happened just about the midnight of their captivity. Thirty-six of the seventy years were now past, and almost as many were yet behind, and now to see their king thus advanced would be a comfortable earnest to them of their own release in due time, in the set time. <hi type="italic">Unto the upright there</hi> thus <hi type="italic">ariseth light in the darkness,</hi> to encourage them to hope, even in the <hi type="italic">cloudy and dark day,</hi> that at <hi type="italic">evening time it shall be light;</hi> when therefore we are perplexed, let us not be in despair.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.25"/> <div eID="gen7611" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen7053" osisID="2Kgs" type="book"/>

entries.88a5644be796f310aef7f78dab6877601073bc78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3606"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 25</title> <div sID="gen5142" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1-2Kgs.25.3">2Ki 25:1-3</reference>. Jerusalem Again Besieged.<div eID="gen5142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3606"/><hi type="bold">1. Nebuchadnezzar ... came ... against Jerusalem--</hi>Incensed by the revolt of Zedekiah, the Assyrian despot determined to put an end to the perfidious and inconstant monarchy of Judea. This chapter narrates his third and last invasion, which he conducted in person at the head of an immense army, levied out of all the tributary nations under his sway. Having overrun the northern parts of the country and taken almost all the fenced cities (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.7">Jr 34:7</reference>), he marched direct to Jerusalem to invest it. The date of the beginning as well as the end of the siege is here carefully marked (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1">Eze 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.1">Jr 39:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.4-Jer.52.6">52:4-6</reference>); from which it appears, that, with a brief interruption caused by Nebuchadnezzar's marching to oppose the Egyptians who were coming to its relief but who retreated without fighting, the siege lasted a year and a half. So long a resistance was owing, not to the superior skill and valor of the Jewish soldiers, but to the strength of the city fortifications, on which the king too confidently relied (compare Jr 21:1-14; 37:1-38:28).<div eID="gen5143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pitched against it, and ... built forts--</hi>rather, perhaps, drew lines of circumvallation, with a ditch to prevent any going out of the city. On this rampart were erected his military engines for throwing missiles into the city. <div eID="gen5144" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1ace72f852214149662c929969833fda2ad39f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3607"/><div sID="gen5145" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3607"/><hi type="bold">3. on the ninth day of the fourth month the famine prevailed--</hi>In consequence of the close and protracted blockade, the inhabitants were reduced to dreadful extremities; and under the maddening influence of hunger, the most inhuman atrocities were perpetrated (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">La 2:20</reference>, 22; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.9">4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">Eze 5:10</reference>). This was a fulfilment of the prophetic denunciations threatened on the apostasy of the chosen people (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">Le 26:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.53-Deut.28.57">De 28:53-57</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.2">Jr 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.13">27:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.16">Eze 4:16</reference>).<div eID="gen5145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5146" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.4-2Kgs.25.30">2Ki 25:4-30</reference>. Zedekiah Taken. <div eID="gen5146" type="x-p"/>
entries.311d502c46f319812c84f2afdb5c6caac8fe6aad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3608"/><div sID="gen5147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3608"/><hi type="bold">4. the city was broken up--</hi>that is, a breach was effected, as we are elsewhere informed, in a part of the wall belonging to the lower city (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.5">2Ch 32:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.14">33:14</reference>).<div eID="gen5147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between two walls, which is by the king's garden--</hi>The king's garden was (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Ne 3:15</reference>) at the pool of Siloam, that is, at the mouth of the Tyropæon. A trace of the outermost of these walls appears to be still extant in the rude pathway which crosses the mouth of the Tyropæon, on a mound hard by the old mulberry tree, which marks the traditional spot of Isaiah's martyrdom [Robinson]. It is probable that the besiegers had overlooked this pass.<div eID="gen5148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king went ... toward the plain--</hi>that is, the Ghor, or valley of Jordan, estimated at five hours' distance from Jerusalem. The plain near Jericho is about eleven or twelve miles broad. <div eID="gen5149" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ab7a4b4d247784b8b97eea368d19f1ff407ac00: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3609"/><div sID="gen5150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3609"/><hi type="bold">6-7. they took the king, and brought him ... to Riblah--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar, having gone from the siege to oppose the auxiliary forces of Pharaoh-hophra, left his generals to carry on the blockade, he himself not returning to the scene of action, but taking up his station at Riblah in the land of Hamath (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.33">2Ki 23:33</reference>).<div eID="gen5150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they gave judgment upon him--</hi>They, that is, the council (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.3">Jr 39:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.6.7">Da 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">8, 12</reference>), regarding him as a seditious and rebellious vassal, condemned him for violating his oath and neglecting the announcement of the divine will as made known to him by Jeremiah (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.32.5">Jr 32:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.2">34:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.17">38:17</reference>). His sons and the nobles who had joined in his flight were slain before his eyes (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.6">Jr 39:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.10">52:10</reference>). In conformity with Eastern ideas, which consider a blind man incapable of ruling, his eyes were put out, and being put in chains, he was carried to perpetual imprisonment in Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jr 52:11</reference>), which, though he came to it, as Ezekiel had foretold, he did not see (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.5">Jr 32:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.16">17:16</reference>). <div eID="gen5151" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b90959b7266a2dfd12331cc4b6479016a805db1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3610"/><div sID="gen5152" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3610"/><hi type="bold">8-18. on the seventh day of the month ... came Nebuzar-adan--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12">Jr 52:12</reference>). In attempting to reconcile these two passages, it must be supposed either that, though he had set out on the seventh, he did not arrive in Jerusalem till the tenth, or that he did not put his orders in execution till that day. His office as captain of the guard (<reference osisRef="Gen.37.36">Ge 37:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.39.1">39:1</reference>) called him to execute the awards of justice on criminals; and hence, although not engaged in the siege of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.13">Jr 39:13</reference>), Nebuzar-adan was despatched to rase the city, to plunder the temple, to lay both in ruins, demolish the fortifications, and transport the inhabitants to Babylon. The most eminent of these were taken to the king at Riblah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.27">2Ki 25:27</reference>) and executed, as instigators and abettors of the rebellion, or otherwise obnoxious to the Assyrian government. In their number were Seraiah, the high priest, grandfather of Ezra (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.1">Ezr 7:1</reference>), his sagan or deputy, a priest of the second order (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jr 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.25">29:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">37:3</reference>). <div eID="gen5152" type="x-p"/>
entries.3cc166c02e54aed71a56c3a92e8ea6bd9f68e190: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3612"/><div sID="gen5154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3612"/><hi type="bold">19. five men of them that were in the king's presence--</hi>that is, who belonged to the royal retinue. It is probable that there were five at first, and that other two were found afterwards (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.25">Jr 52:25</reference>). <div eID="gen5154" type="x-p"/>
entries.e64c89822aabb8b149b3d11e21f6c38fea6b520c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3613"/><div sID="gen5155" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3613"/><hi type="bold">22-26. Nebuchadnezzar ... made Gedaliah ... ruler--</hi>The people permitted to remain were, besides the king's daughters, a few court attendants and others (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.7">Jr 40:7</reference>) too insignificant to be removed, only the peasantry who could till the land and dress the vineyards. Gedaliah was Jeremiah's friend (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.24">Jr 26:24</reference>), and having, by the prophet's counsel, probably fled from the city as abandoned of God, he surrendered himself to the conqueror (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.2">Jr 38:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.17">17</reference>), and being promoted to the government of Judea, fixed his provincial court at Mizpeh. He was well qualified to surmount the difficulties of ruling at such a crisis. Many of the fugitive Jews, as well as the soldiers of Zedekiah who had accompanied the king in his flight to the plains of Jericho, left their retreats (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.11">Jr 40:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.12">12</reference>) and flocked around the governor; who having counselled them to submit, promised them on complying with this condition, security on oath that they would retain their possessions and enjoy the produce of their land (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.9">Jr 40:9</reference>). <div eID="gen5155" type="x-p"/>
entries.51c928c0fc67cee12f327366f1e57a34051cec08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3616"/><div sID="gen5158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3616"/><hi type="bold">27. seven and thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin--</hi>corresponding with the year of Nebuchadnezzar's death, and his son Evil-merodach's ascension to the throne.<div eID="gen5158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Evil-merodach ... did lift up the head of Jehoiachin ... and spake kindly--</hi>gave him liberty upon parole. This kindly feeling is said to have originated in a familiar acquaintance formed in prison, in which Evil-merodach had lain till his father's death, on account of some malversation while acting as regent during Nebuchadnezzar's seven years' illness (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.32">Da 4:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.33">33</reference>). But doubtless the improvement in Zedekiah's condition is to be traced to the overruling providence and grace of Him who still cherished purposes of love to the house of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14">2Sa 7:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.15">15</reference>). <div eID="gen5159" type="x-p"/>
entries.040c67761092e286f9180a65cc9dc0716b4ef6dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3617"/><div sID="gen5160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3617"/><hi type="bold">29. Jehoiachin ... did eat ... continually before him--</hi>According to an ancient usage in Eastern courts, had a seat at the royal table on great days, and had a stated provision granted him for the maintenance of his exiled court. <chapter eID="2Kgs.25"/><div eID="gen5160" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen4675" osisID="2Kgs" type="book"/>

entries.12d62eaa75c4f27cbd82929fec7a18d55565e2b2: <div eID="gen13305" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13306" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem; it is taken, after having been sorely reduced by famine, etc.; and Zedekiah, endeavoring to make his escape, is made prisoner, his sons slain before his eyes; then, his eyes being put out, he is put in chains and carried to Babylon, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1-2Kgs.25.7">2Kgs 25:1-7</reference>. Nebuzar-adan burns the temple, breaks down the walls of Jerusalem, and carries away the people captives, leaving only a few to till the ground, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.8-2Kgs.25.12">2Kgs 25:8-12</reference>. He takes away all the brass, and all the vessels of the temple, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.13-2Kgs.25.17">2Kgs 25:13-17</reference>. Several of the chief men and nobles found in the city, he brings to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, who puts them all to death, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18-2Kgs.25.21">2Kgs 25:18-21</reference>. Nebuchadnezzar makes Gedaliah governor over the poor people that were left, against whom Ishmael rises, and slays him, and others with him; on which the people in general, fearing the resentment of the Chaldeans, flee to Egypt, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.22-2Kgs.25.26">2Kgs 25:22-26</reference>. Evil-merodach, king of Babylon, releases Jehoiachin out of prison, treats him kindly, and makes him his friend, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.27-2Kgs.25.30">2Kgs 25:27-30</reference>.
entries.064565a9ecbab378edfafa7d3599a803b9f5ecb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen13323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13324" type="x-p"/> And the city was besieged, etc. - Nebuchadnezzar, having routed the Egyptian army, returned to Jerusalem, and besieged it so closely that, being reduced by famine, and a breach made in the wall, the Chaldeans entered it on the ninth day of the fourth month, (Wednesday, July 27), Zedekiah and many others endeavoring to make their escape by night.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.25"/> <div eID="gen13324" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen12392" osisID="2Kgs" type="book"/>
entries.e19ac957110d62736f46ee675cbfa16898b7dab3: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen13306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13307" type="x-p"/> The army of the Chaldeans pursued - Zedekiah was taken, and brought captive to Riblah in Syria, where Nebuchadnezzar then lay, who ordered his sons to be slain before his face, and then put out his eyes; and having loaded him with chains, sent him to Babylon, (see <reference osisRef="Jer.39.4">Jer 39:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.7">Jer 39:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.7">Jer 52:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jer 52:11</reference>), thus fulfilling the prophetic declarations, that his eyes should see the eyes of the king of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.4">Jer 32:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.3">Jer 34:3</reference>; but Babylon he should not see, though he was to die there; <reference osisRef="Eze.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>.
entries.3e3f372e527d7d2b9f97f16af8d04876a298532f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen13307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13308" type="x-p"/> In the fifth month - On the seventh day of the fifth month, (answering to Wednesday, Aug. 24), Nebuzar-adan made his entry into the city; and having spent two days in making provision, on the tenth day of the same month, (Saturday, Aug. 27), he set fire to the temple and the king's palace, and the houses of the nobility, and burnt them to the ground; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.13">Jer 52:13</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Jer.39.8">Jer 39:8</reference>. Thus the temple was destroyed in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar, the first of the XLVIIIth Olympiad, in the one hundred and sixtieth current year of the era of Nabonassar, four hundred and twenty-four years three months and eight days from the time in which Solomon laid its foundation stone.
entries.f2afd531c0905ef7bc1ad914ca9bd989df2c1f1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen13308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13309" type="x-p"/> Brake down the walls - In the same fifth month, <reference osisRef="Jer.1.3">Jer 1:3</reference>, the walls of Jerusalem being razed to the ground, all that were left in the city, and all that had fled over formerly to Nebuchadnezzar, and all the common people of the city, with all the king's treasures, those of the nobles, and the whole furniture of the temple, did Nebuzar-adan carry off to Babylon. See <reference osisRef="Jer.39.8">Jer 39:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">Jer 39:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.14">Jer 52:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.23">Jer 52:23</reference>. And thus was Judah carried away out of her own land, four hundred and sixty-eight years after David began to reign over it; from the division of the ten tribes three hundred and eighty-eight years; and from the destruction of the kingdom of Israel, one hundred and thirty-four years; A.M. 3416, and before Christ five hundred and ninety. And thus ends what is called the fifth age of the world. See Usher's Annals.
entries.c4fb4308d2ae8c97ec9f14464740dac7a07ac934: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen13309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13310" type="x-p"/> Seraiah the chief priest - Zephaniah - The person who is here called the second priest was what the Jews call sagan, a sort of deputy, who performed the functions of the high priest when he was prevented by any infirmity from attending the temple service. See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4">2Kgs 23:4</reference> (note).
entries.365ee394d6d1b003fecc8ac85e8edf8e5d831e18: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen13310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13311" type="x-p"/> And five men of them that were in the king's presence - These were principal counselors, and confidential officers. <div eID="gen13311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13312" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Jer.52.25">Jer 52:25</reference>, it is said he took seven men who were near the king's person, and the same number is found in the Arabic in this place; and the Chaldee has no less than fifty men; but in Jeremiah this, as well as all the rest of the versions, reads seven. Probably they were no more than five at first, or, perhaps Jeremiah reckoned with the five the officer that was set over the men of war, and the principal scribe of the host mentioned here, as two with the five; and thus made seven in the whole.
entries.18f0a8df5d4f69b304103d7b93b47319934d430f: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen13312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13313" type="x-p"/> The king of Babylon smote them - He had, no doubt, found that these had counselled Zedekiah to revolt.
entries.bfc886e8103055ef26ba26539465134b3eaadc41: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen13313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13314" type="x-p"/> Made Gedaliah - ruler - This was no regal dignity; he was only a sort of hind or overseer, appointed to regulate the husbandmen.
entries.5582c2c1ae432b15f4211f73cf375ecf8891b1ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen13314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13315" type="x-p"/> To Mizpah - This is said to have been situated on the east side of the river Jordan, and most contiguous to Babylon, and therefore the most proper for the residence of Gedaliah, because nearest to the place from which he was to receive his instructions. But there were several places of this name, and we do not exactly know where this was situated.
entries.65d74985552ad5cff52600ec3e03c823103b3603: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen13315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13316" type="x-p"/> Gedaliah sware to them - He pledged himself in the most solemn manner to encourage and protect them.
entries.06b848f3f057fe404cbe047075645e5922256ea5: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen13316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13317" type="x-p"/> Smote Gedaliah - This was at an entertainment which Gedaliah had made for them; see <reference osisRef="Jer.41.1">Jer 41:1</reference>, etc. He was not content with this murder, but slew fourscore more, who were coming with offerings to the temple, and took several as prisoners, among whom were some of the king's daughters; and set off to go to the Ammonites: but Johanan, the son of Careah, hearing of these outrages, raised a number of men, and pursued Ishmael upon which Ishmael's prisoners immediately turned and joined Johanan; so that he, and eight of his accomplices, with difficulty escaped to the Ammonites. See <reference osisRef="Jer.41.1">Jer 41:1</reference>, etc. Baalis, king of the Ammonites, had sent Ishmael to murder Gedaliah; and of this he was informed by Johanan, who offered to prevent it, by taking away the life of this murderer. But Gedaliah could not believe that he harbored such foul designs, and therefore took no precaution to save his life. See <reference osisRef="Jer.40.13-Jer.40.16">Jer 40:13-16</reference>.
entries.f094d4acfc6683a89a61f6a9fabeb6e21f9d2669: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen13317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13318" type="x-p"/> And it came to pass - Nebuchadnezzar was just now dead; and Evil-merodach, his son, succeeded to the kingdom in the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin: and on the seven and twentieth day [Jeremiah says five and twentieth] of the twelfth month of that year, (Tuesday, April 15, A.M. 3442), he brought the long captivated Jewish king out of prison; treated him kindly; and ever after, during his life, reckoned him among the king's friends. This is particularly related in the four last verses of the book of Jeremiah.
entries.8ba0a196e89a82fd749412546777c52fbffa993e: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen13318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13319" type="x-p"/> A continual allowance given him of the king - He lived in a regal style, and had his court even in the city of Babylon, being supplied with every requisite by the munificence and friendship of the king. In about two years after this, Evil-merodach was slain in a conspiracy; and it is supposed that Jehoiachin, then about fifty-eight years of age, fell with his friend and protector. Thus terminates the catastrophe of the Jewish kings, people, and state; the consequence of unheard-of rebellions and provocations against the Majesty of heaven. <div eID="gen13319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13320" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13321" type="x-p"/> In the ninth year of his reign - Zedekiah, having revolted against the Chaldeans, Nebuchadnezzar, wearied with his treachery, and the bad faith of the Jews, determined the total subversion of the Jewish state. Having assembled a numerous army, he entered Judea on the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year of the reign of Zedekiah; this, according to the computation of Archbishop Usher, was on Thursday, January 30, A.M. 3414, which was a sabbatical year: whereon the men of Jerusalem hearing that the Chaldean army was approaching, proclaimed liberty to their servants; see <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8-Jer.34.10">Jer 34:8-10</reference>, according to the law, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.2">Exo 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.15.1">Deu 15:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.2">Deu 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.12">Deu 15:12</reference> : for Nebuchadnezzar, marching with his army against Zedekiah, having wasted all the country, and taken their strong holds, except Lachish, Azekah, and Jerusalem, came against the latter with all his forces. See <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1-Jer.34.7">Jer 34:1-7</reference>. On the very day, as the same author computes, the siege and utter destruction of Jerusalem were revealed to Ezekiel the prophet, then in Chaldea, under the type of a seething pot; and his wife died in the evening, and he was charged not to mourn for her, because of the extraordinary calamity that had fallen upon the land. See <reference osisRef="Eze.24.1">Eze 24:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.24.2">Eze 24:2</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen13321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13322" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah, having predicted the same calamities, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1-Jer.34.7">Jer 34:1-7</reference>, was by the command of Zedekiah shut up in prison, Jeremiah 32:1-16. <div eID="gen13322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13323" type="x-p"/> Pharaoh Hophra, or Vaphris, hearing how Zedekiah was pressed, and fearing for the safety of his own dominions should the Chaldeans succeed against Jerusalem, determined to succor Zedekiah. Finding this, the Chaldeans raised the siege of Jerusalem, and went to meet the Egyptian army, which they defeated and put to flight. Joseph. Antiq., lib. 10, cap. 10. In the interim the Jews, thinking their danger was passed, reclaimed their servants, and put them again under the yoke; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8">Jer 34:8</reference>, etc.

entries.9cf46d4d439bd465d9031ecc358a67c91dadacea: <hi type="italic">Siege and conquest of Jerusalem; Zedekiah taken prisoner and led away to Babel</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.52.4-Jer.52.11">Jer 52:4-11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.39.1-Jer.39.7">Jer 39:1-7</reference>). - 2Ki 25:1. In the ninth year of the reign of Zedekiah, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar marched with all his forces against Jerusalem and commenced the siege (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.39.1">Jer 39:1</reference>), after he had taken all the rest of the fortified cities of the land, with the exception of Lachish and Azekah, which were besieged at the same time as Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.7">Jer 34:7</reference>). On the very same day the commencement of the siege of Jerusalem was revealed to the prophet Ezekiel in his exile (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1">Eze 24:1</reference>). “And they built against it (the city) siege-towers round about.” דּיק, which only occurs here and in Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.4">Jer 52:4</reference>) and Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.2">Eze 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.17">Eze 17:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.27">Eze 21:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.8">Eze 26:8</reference>), does not mean either a line of circumvallation (J. D. Mich., Hitzig), or the outermost enclosure constructed of palisades (Thenius, whose assertion that דּיק is always mentioned as the first work of the besiegers is refuted by <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.17">Eze 17:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.27">Eze 21:27</reference>), but a watch, and that in a collective sense: watch-towers or siege-towers (cf. Ges. <hi type="italic">thes.</hi> p. 330, and Hävernick on <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.2">Eze 4:2</reference>).
entries.67f419e4ba0905d21f80c252d2f08deeff4d32e9: 2Ki 25:2 “And the city was besieged till the eleventh year of king Zedekiah,” in which the northern wall of the city was broken through on the ninth day of the fourth month (2Ki 25:3). That Jerusalem could sustain a siege of this duration, namely eighteen months, shows what the strength of the fortifications must have been. Moreover the siege was interrupted for a short time, when the approach of the Egyptian king Hophra compelled the Chaldaeans to march to meet him and drive him back, which they appear to have succeeded in doing without a battle (cf. Jer 37:5., <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.7">Eze 17:7</reference>).
entries.da0d438f51c8402ace0e4e97859a9c15613dd383: 2Ki 25:3-4 <div eID="gen5502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5503" type="x-p"/> Trusting partly to the help of the Egyptians and partly to the strength of Jerusalem, Zedekiah paid no attention to the repeated entreaties of Jeremiah, that he would save himself with his capital and people from the destruction which was otherwise inevitable, by submitting, to the Chaldaeans (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.38.17">Jer 38:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.18">Jer 38:18</reference>), but allowed things to reach their worst, until the famine became so intense, that inhuman horrors were perpetrated (cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.2.20-Lam.2.21">Lam 2:20-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.9-Lam.4.10">Lam 4:9-10</reference>), and eventually a breach was made in the city wall on the ninth day of the fourth month. The statement of the month is omitted in our text, where the words הרביעי בּחרשׁ (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.6">Jer 52:6</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.39.2">Jer 39:2</reference>) have fallen out before בּתשׁעה (2Ki 25:3, commencement) through the oversight of a copyist. The overwhelming extent of the famine is mentioned, not “because the people were thereby rendered quite unfit to offer any further resistance” (Seb. Schm.), but as a proof of the truth of the prophetic announcements (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">Lev 26:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.53-Deut.28.57">Deu 28:53-57</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.2">Jer 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.13">Jer 27:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.16-Ezek.4.17">Eze 4:16-17</reference>). הארץ עם are the common people in Jerusalem, or the citizens of the capital. From the more minute account of the entrance of the enemy into the city in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.3-Jer.39.5">Jer 39:3-5</reference> we learn that the Chaldaeans made a breach in the northern or outer wall of the lower city, i.e., the second wall, built by Hezekiah and Manasseh (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.5">2Ch 32:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.14">2Ch 33:14</reference>), and forced their way into the lower city (המּשׁנה, 2Ki 22:14), so that their generals took their stand at the gate of the centre, which was in the wall that separated the lower city from the upper city upon Zion, and formed the passage from the one to the other. When Zedekiah saw them here, he fled by night with the soldiers out of the city, through the gate between the two walls at or above the king’s garden, on the road to the plain of the Jordan, while the Chaldaeans were round about the city. In 2Ki 25:4 a faulty text has come down to us. In the clause המּלחמה וכל־אנשׁי the verb יברחוּ is omitted, if not even more, namely העיר מן ויּצאוּ יברחוּ, “fled and went out of the city.” And if we compare <reference osisRef="Jer.39.4">Jer 39:4</reference>, it is evident that before הם וכל־אנשׁיstill more has dropped out, not merely המּלך, which must have stood in the text, since according to 2Ki 25:5 the king was among the fugitives; but most probably the whole clause יהוּדה מלך צדקיּהוּ ראם כּאשׁר ויהי, since the words הם וכל־אנשׁי have no real connection with what precedes, and cannot form a circumstantial clause so far as the sense is concerned. The “gate between the two walls, which (was) at or over (על) the king’s garden,” was a gate at the mouth of the Tyropoeon, that is to say, at the south-eastern corner of the city of Zion; for, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference>, the king’s garden was at the pool of Siloah, i.e., at the mouth of the Tyropoeon (see Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> ii. 142). By this defile, therefore, the approach to the city was barred by a double wall, the inner one running from Zion to the Ophel, whilst the outer one, at some distance off, connected the Zion wall with the outer surrounding wall of the Ophel, and most probably enclosed the king’s garden. The subject to ויּלך is המּלך, which has dropped out before הם וכל־אנשׁי. הערבה is the lowland valley on both sides of the Jordan (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.1.1">Deu 1:1</reference>).
entries.5bdce43030e477ac8e7a420b43b2972a49fac605: 2Ki 25:5 <div eID="gen5503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5504" type="x-p"/> As the Chaldaeans were encamped around the city, the flight was immediately discovered. The Chaldaean army pursued him, and overtook him in the steppes of Jericho, whilst his own army was dispersed, all of which Ezekiel had foreseen in the Spirit (Eze 12:3.). ירחו ערבות are that portion of the plain of the Jordan which formed the country round Jericho (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.4.13">Jos 4:13</reference>).
entries.7f31ad9e9a872d24e213de14e956e44174d2a38e: 2Ki 25:6 <div eID="gen5504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5505" type="x-p"/> Zedekiah having been seized by the Chaldaeans, was taken to the king of Babel in the Chaldaean headquarters at Riblah (see at 2Ki 23:33), and was there put upon his trial. According to 2Ki 25:1, Nebuchadnezzar had commenced the siege of Jerusalem in person; but afterwards, possibly not till after the Egyptians who came to relieve the besieged city had been repulsed, he transferred the continuance of the siege, which was a prolonged one, to his generals, and retired to Riblah, to conduct the operations of the whole campaign from thence. את־פל משׁפּט דּבּר, to conduct judicial proceedings with any one, i.e., to hear and judge him. For this Jeremiah constantly uses the plural משׁפּטם, not only in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.9">Jer 52:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.39.5">Jer 39:5</reference>, but also in <reference osisRef="Jer.1.16">Jer 1:16</reference> and Jer 4:12.
entries.2c7073ae79ec39939d20ac4643032e2e1ec74072: 2Ki 25:7 <div eID="gen5505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5506" type="x-p"/> The punishment pronounced upon Zedekiah was the merited reward of the breach of his oath, and his hardening himself against the counsel of the Lord which was announced to him by Jeremiah during the siege, that he should save not only his own life, but also Jerusalem from destruction, by a voluntary submission to the Chaldaeans, whereas by obstinate resistance he would bring an ignominious destruction upon himself, his family, the city, and the whole people (Jer 38:17., <reference osisRef="Jer.32.5">Jer 32:5</reference>; Jer 34:3.). His sons, who, though not mentioned in 2Ki 25:4, had fled with him and had been taken, and (according to <reference osisRef="Jer.52.10">Jer 52:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.39.6">Jer 39:6</reference>) all the nobles (princes) of Judah, sc. those who had fled with the king, were slain before his eyes. He himself was then blinded, and led away to Babel, chained with double chains of brass, and kept a prisoner there till his death (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jer 52:11</reference>); so that, as Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>) had prophesied, he came to Babel, but did not see the land, and died there. Blinding by pricking out the eyes was a common punishment for princes among the Babylonians and Persians (cf. Herod. vii. 18, and Brisson, <hi type="italic">de region Pers. princip.</hi> p. 589). נחשׁתּים, double brazen chains, are brazen fetters for the hands and feet. Samson was treated in the same manner by the Philistines (Jdg 16:21).<hi type="italic">Destruction of Jerusalem and the temple.</hi> The people carried away to Babel (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12-Jer.52.27">Jer 52:12-27</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.39.8-Jer.39.10">Jer 39:8-10</reference>). - In this section we have first a general account of the destruction of the temple and city (2Ki 25:8-10), and of the carrying away of the people (2Ki 25:11 and 2Ki 25:12), and then a more particular description of what was done with the metal vessels of the temple (2Ki 25:13-17), and how the spiritual and secular leaders of the people who had been taken prisoners were treated (2Ki 25:18-21).
entries.6a765dfaed06ad244ed2a4dec4cb6d568ff3fc96: 2Ki 25:8-10 <div eID="gen5506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5507" type="x-p"/> The destruction of Jerusalem, by the burning of the temple, of the king’s palace, and of all the larger buildings, and by throwing down the walls, was effected by Nebuzaradan, the chief of the body-guard of Nebuchadnezzar, on the seventh day of the fifth month in the nineteenth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. Instead of the <hi type="italic">seventh</hi> day we have the <hi type="italic">tenth</hi> in Jer 52:12. This difference might be reconciled, as proposed by earlier commentators, on the assumption that the burning of the city lasted several days, commencing on the seventh and ending on the tenth. But since there are similar differences met with afterwards (2Ki 25:17, 2Ki 25:19) in the statement of numbers, which can only be accounted for from the substitution of similar numeral letters, we must assume that there is a change of this kind here. Which of the two dates is the correct one it is impossible to determine. The circumstance that the later Jews kept the ninth as a fast-day cannot be regarded as decisive evidence in favour of the date given in Jeremiah, as Thenius supposes; for in Zec 7:3 and Zec 8:19 the fasting of the fifth month is mentioned, but no day is given; and though in the Talmudic times the ninth day of the month began to be kept as a fast-day, this was not merely in remembrance of the Chaldaean destruction of Jerusalem, but of the Roman also, and of three other calamities which had befallen the nation (see the statement of the Gemara on this subject in Lightfoot, <hi type="italic">Opp.</hi> ii. p. 139, ed. Leusden, and in Köhler on Zec 7:3), from which we see that the Gemarists in the most unhistorical manner grouped together different calamitous events in one single day. The nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar corresponds to the eleventh of Zedekiah (see at 2Ki 24:12). Nebuzaradan is not mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.3">Jer 39:3</reference> among the Chaldaean generals who forced their way into the city, so that he must have been ordered to Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar after the taking of the city and the condemnation of Zedekiah, to carry out the destruction of the city, the carrying away of the people, and the appointment of a deputy-governor over those who were left behind in the land. This explains in a very simple manner how a month could intervene between their forcing their way into the city, at all events into the lower city, and the burning of it to the ground, without there being any necessity to assume, with Thenius, that the city of Zion held out for a month, which is by no means probable, for the simple reason that the fighting men had fled with Zedekiah and had been scattered in their flight. רב־תבּחים = הטּבּחים שׂר in <reference osisRef="Gen.37.36">Gen 37:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.39.1">Gen 39:1</reference>, was with the Babylonians, as with the Egyptians, the chief of the king’s body-guard, whose duty it was to execute the sentences of death (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.37.36">Gen 37:36</reference>). הטּבּחים answers to the הכּרתי of the Israelites (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:18</reference>, etc.). In <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12">Jer 52:12</reference> we have מלך לפני עמד instead of מלך עבד, without the אשׁר, which is rarely omitted in prose, and בּירוּשׁלם instead of ירוּשׁלם: he came into Jerusalem, not he forced a way into the real Jerusalem (Thenius). The meaning is not altered by these two variations.
entries.e03ae630e5d4b21db87def520e79edc1726a0b7e: 2Ki 25:11-12 <div eID="gen5508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5509" type="x-p"/> The rest of the people he led away, both those who had been left behind in the city and the deserters who had gone over to the Chaldaeans, and the remnant of the multitude. ההמון יתר, for which we have האמון יתר in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.15">Jer 52:15</reference>, has been interpreted in various ways. As אמון signifies an artist or artificer in <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Pro 8:30</reference>, and העם יתר has just preceded it, we might be disposed to give the preference to the reading האמון, as Hitzig and Graf have done, and understand by it the remnant of the artisans, who were called והמּסגּר החרשׁ in 2Ki 24:14, 2Ki 24:16. But this view is precluded by <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">Jer 39:9</reference>, where we find הנּשׁארים העם יתר instead of האמון יתר or ההמון .י These words cannot be set aside by the arbitrary assumption that they crept into the text through a copyist’s error; for the assertion that they contain a purposeless repetition is a piece of dogmatical criticism, inasmuch as there is a distinction drawn in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">Jer 39:9</reference> between בּעיר הנּשׁארים העם יתר העם הןּ and הנּשׁארים העם יתר. Consequently האמון is simply another form for ההמון (ה and א being interchanged) in the sense of a mass of people, and we have simply the choice left between two interpretations. Either בּעיר הנּשׁארים העם יתר means the fighting people left in the city, as distinguished from the deserters who had fled to the Chaldaeans, and האמון = ההמון יתר in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.15">Jer 52:15</reference>, or הנּשׁארים העם יתר in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">Jer 39:9</reference>, the rest of the inhabitants of Jerusalem; or בּעיר הנּשׁ העם יתר is the people left in Jerusalem (warriors and non-warriors), and ההמון יתר the rest of the population of the land outside Jerusalem. The latter is probably the preferable view, not only because full justice is thereby done to בּעיר in the first clause, but also because it is evident from the exception mentioned in 2Ki 25:12 that the deportation was not confined to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, but extended to the population of the whole land. The “poor people,” whom he allowed to remain in the land as vine-dressers and husbandmen, were the common people, or people without property, not merely in Jerusalem, but throughout the whole land. הארץ דּלּת = עם־הארץ דּלּת   (2Ki 24:14). Instead of מדּלּת we have in Jeremiah מדּלּות: the plural used in an abstract sense, “the poverty,” i.e., the lower people, “the poor who had nothing” (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.10">Jer 39:10</reference>). Instead of the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> לגבים from גּוּב, <hi type="italic">secuit</hi>, <hi type="italic">aravit</hi>, the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> has ליגבים from יגב, in the same sense, after Jer 52:16.
entries.aeac3d1545ce02eaf525b4e36e80c339bbc11423: 2Ki 25:13-17 <div eID="gen5509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5510" type="x-p"/> The brazen vessels of the temple were broken in pieces, and the brass, and smaller vessels of brass, silver, and gold, were carried away. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.52.17-Jer.52.23">Jer 52:17-23</reference>, where several other points are mentioned that have been passed over in the account before us. The pillars of brass (see 1Ki 7:15.), the stands (see 1Ki 7:27.), and the brazen sea (1Ki 7:23.), were broken in pieces, because it would have been difficult to carry these colossal things away without breaking them up. On the smaller vessels used in the worship (2Ki 25:14) see 1Ki 7:40. In <reference osisRef="Jer.52.18">Jer 52:18</reference> המּזרקת are also mentioned. 2Ki 25:15 is abridged still more in contrast with <reference osisRef="Jer.52.19">Jer 52:19</reference>, and only המּחתּות and המּזרקות are mentioned, whereas in Jeremiah six different things are enumerated beside the candlesticks. כּסף...זהב אשׁר, “what was of gold, gold, what was of silver, silver, the captain of the guard took away,” is a comprehensive description of the objects carried away. To this there is appended a remark in 2Ki 25:16 concerning the quantity of the brass of the large vessels, which was so great that it could not be weighed; and in 2Ki 25:17 a supplementary notice respecting the artistic work of the two pillars of brass. וגו העמּוּדים is placed at the head absolutely: as for the pillars, etc., the brass of all these vessels was not to be weighed. In <reference osisRef="Jer.52.20">Jer 52:20</reference>, along with the brazen sea, the twelve brazen oxen under it are mentioned; and in the description of the pillars of brass (Jer 52:21.) there are several points alluded to which are omitted in our books, not only here, but also in 1Ki 7:16. For the fact itself see the explanation given there. The omission of the twelve oxen in so condensed an account as that contained in our text does not warrant the inference that these words in Jeremiah are a spurious addition made by a later copyist, since the assumption that Ahaz sent the brazen oxen to king Tiglath-pileser cannot be proved from 2Ki 16:17. Instead of אמּה שׁלשׁ we must read אמּת המשׁ, five <hi type="italic">cubits</hi>, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.52.22">Jer 52:22</reference> and 1Ki 7:16. The על־השּׂבכה at the end of the verse is very striking, since it stands quite alone, and when connected with וגו וכאלּה does not appear to yield any appropriate sense, as the second pillar was like the first not merely with regard to the trellis-work, but in its form and size throughout. At the same time, it is possible that the historian intended to give especial prominence to the similarity of the two pillars with reference to this one point alone.
entries.6de43799bf697b97dbe0c5cbdfd66d13930e269f: 2Ki 25:18-21 (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.52.24-Jer.52.27">Jer 52:24-27</reference>). The principal officers of the temple and city, and sixty men of the population of the land, who were taken at the destruction of Jerusalem, Nebuzaradan sent to his king at Riblah, where they were put to death. <hi type="italic">Seraiah</hi>, the high priest, is the grandfather or great-grandfather of Ezra the scribe (Ezr 7:1; <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.14">1Ch 6:14</reference>). <hi type="italic">Zephaniah</hi>, a priest of the second rank (משׁנה כּהן; in Jer. המּשׁנה כּהן: see at 2Ki 23:4), is probably the same person as the son of Maaseiah, who took a prominent place among the priests, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jer 21:1</reference>; Jer 29:25., and Jer 37:3. The “three keepers of the threshold” are probably the three superintendents of the Levites, whose duty it was to keep guard over the temple, and therefore were among the principal officers of the sanctuary.
