entries.380a20a7cad1f57ecf2ea3c18080a84fc4e48941: 2Ki 25:22-23 <div eID="gen5511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5512" type="x-p"/> Over the remnant of the people left in the land Nebuchadnezzar placed Gedaliah as governor of the land, who took up his abode in Mizpah. <hi type="italic">Gedaliah</hi>, the son of Ahikam, who had interested himself on behalf of the prophet Jeremiah and saved his life (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.24">Jer 26:24</reference>), and the grandson of Shaphan, a man of whom nothing more is known (see at 2Ki 22:12), had his home in Jerusalem, and, as we may infer from his attitude towards Jeremiah, had probably secured the confidence of the Chaldaeans at the siege and conquest of Jerusalem by his upright conduct, and by what he did to induce the people to submit to the judgment inflicted by God; so that Nebuchadnezzar entrusted him with the oversight of those who were left behind in the land-men, women, children, poor people, and even a few princesses and court-officials, whom they had not thought it necessary or worth while to carry away (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.7">Jer 40:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.10">Jer 41:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.41.16">Jer 41:16</reference>), i.e., he made him governor of the conquered land. Mizpah is the present <hi type="italic">Nebi Samwil</hi>, two hours to the north-west of Jerusalem (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.26">Jos 18:26</reference>). - On hearing of Gedaliah’s appointment as governor, there came to him “all the captains of the several divisions of the army and their men,” i.e., those portions of the army which had been scattered at the flight of the king (2Ki 25:5), and which had escaped from the Chaldaeans, and, as it is expressed in <reference osisRef="Jer.40.7">Jer 40:7</reference>, had dispersed themselves “in the field,” i.e., about the land. Instead of והאנשׁים we have in <reference osisRef="Jer.40.7">Jer 40:7</reference> the clearer expression ואנשׁיהם, “and their men,” whilst והאנשׁים in our text receives its more precise definition from the previous word החילים. Of the military commanders the following are mentioned by name: Ishmael, etc. (the ו eht( .cte ,l before ישׁמעאל, is explic., “and indeed Ishmael”). Ishmael, son of Mattaniah and grandson of Elishama, probably of the king’s secretary mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.36.12">Jer 36:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.36.20">Jer 36:20</reference>, of royal blood. Nothing further is known about the other names. We simply learn from Jer 40:13. that Johanan had warned Gedaliah against the treachery of Ishmael, and that when Gedaliah was slain by Ishmael, having disregarded the warning, he put himself at the head of the people and marched with them to Egypt, notwithstanding the dissuasions of Jeremiah (Jer 41:15.). Instead of “Johanan the son of Kareah,” we have in <reference osisRef="Jer.40.8">Jer 40:8</reference> “Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah;” but it is uncertain whether ויונתן has crept into the text of Jeremiah from the previous יהוחנן merely through a mistake, and this mistake has brought with it the alteration of בּן into בּני (Ewald), or whether ויונתן has dropped out of our text through an oversight, and this omission has occasioned the alteration of בני into בן (Thenius, Graf, etc.). The former supposition is favoured by the circumstance that in <reference osisRef="Jer.40.13">Jer 40:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.11">Jer 41:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.41.16">Jer 41:16</reference>, Johanan the son of Kareah alone is mentioned. In <reference osisRef="Jer.40.8">Jer 40:8</reference> עופי וּבני (<hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> עיפי) stands before הנּטפתי, according to which it was not Seraiah who sprang from Netophah, but Ophai whose sons were military commanders. He was called <hi type="italic">Netophathite</hi> because he sprang from <hi type="italic">Netopha</hi> in the neighbourhood of Bethlehem (<reference osisRef="Neh.7.26">Neh 7:26</reference>; Ezr 2:22), the identity of which with <hi type="italic">Beit Nettif</hi> is by no means probable (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.28">2Sa 23:28</reference>). The name יאזביהוּ is written יזניהוּ in Jeremiah; he was the son of the Maachathite, i.e., his father sprang from the Syrian district of Maacah in the neighbourhood of the Hermon (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference>).
entries.530329aaef5ae76478ab1183b9778019a8fcca17: 2Ki 25:24 <div eID="gen5512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5513" type="x-p"/> As these men were afraid of the vengeance of the Chaldaeans because they had fought against them, Gedaliah assured them on oath that they had nothing to fear from them if they would dwell peaceably in the land, be submissive to the king of Babel, and cultivate the land (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.40.9">Jer 40:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.40.10">Jer 40:10</reference>). “Servants of the Chaldees” are Chaldaean officials who were subordinate to the governor Gedaliah.
entries.b0b0e64afc48dca5605dd3806acd4b854fe51b49: 2Ki 25:25 <div eID="gen5513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5514" type="x-p"/> In the seventh month, i.e., hardly two months after the destruction of Jerusalem, came Ishmael with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and murdered him together with the Jews and Chaldaeans, whom he had with him as soldiers to do his bidding and for his protection. This occurred, according to Jer 41:1., when Gedaliah had received them hospitably and had invited them to eat with him. Ishmael was instigated to commit this murder by the Ammonitish king Baalis, and Gedaliah had previously been made acquainted with the intended crime and put upon his guard by Johanan, but had put no faith in the information (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.13-Jer.40.16">Jer 40:13-16</reference>).
entries.e623839384b1efdbc1e3a16a4801c3dc822e28d8: 2Ki 25:26 <div eID="gen5514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5515" type="x-p"/> After Ishmael had performed this deed, and had also treacherously murdered a number of men, who had come to the temple with a sacrifice from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, he took the Jews who were at Mizpah prisoners, with some kings’ daughters among them, intending to take them over to the Ammonites; but as soon as his deed became known, he was pursued by Johanan and the rest of the military chiefs and was overtaken at Gibeon, whereupon those who had been led away by him went over to Johanan, so that he was only able to make his escape with eight men and get away to the Ammonites (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.4-Jer.41.15">Jer 41:4-15</reference>). Johanan then went with the rest of the military commanders and the people whom he had brought back into the neighbourhood of Bethlehem, with the intention of fleeing to Egypt for fear of the Chaldaeans. There they did indeed have recourse to the prophet Jeremiah, to inquire of him the word of the Lord; but they did not allow themselves to be diverted from their intention by the word of the Lord which he announced to them, that if they remained in the land they need not fear anything from the king of Babel, but if they went to Egypt they should all perish there with sword, hunger, and pestilence, or by the prediction that the Lord would also deliver Pharaoh Hophra into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar (Jer 42). They went to Egypt notwithstanding, taking the prophet himself with them, and settled in different cities of Egypt, where they gave themselves up to idolatry, and did not suffer themselves to be drawn away from it even by the severe judgments which the prophet Jeremiah predicted as sure to fall upon them (<reference osisRef="Jer.43.1-Jer.43.13">Jer 43:1-13</reference> and 44). In the verse before us we have simply a brief allusion to the eventual result of the whole affair. “Because they were afraid of the Chaldaeans,” namely, that they might possibly take vengeance upon them for the murder of the governor.
entries.9867316e0e8446ce0b013ecf08ff39b5c5800b88: 2Ki 25:27 <hi type="italic">Jehoiachin delivered from prison, and exalted to royal honours</hi> (cf. Jer. 42:31-34). - In the thirty-seventh year after his deportation Jehoiachin was taken out of prison by Evil-merodach when he came to the throne. מלכו בּשׁנת, in the year of his becoming king, probably immediately after he had ascended the throne, for it was no doubt an act of grace at the commencement of his reign. את־ראשׁ נשׂא, to lift up a persons’ head, i.e., to release him from prison and exalt him to civil honours and dignities (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.40.13">Gen 40:13</reference>). On the coincidence of the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin’s imprisonment and the commencement of the reign of Evil-merodach see the remarks at 2Ki 24:12. Instead of the 27th day of the month, the 25th is given in Jeremiah, again through the substitution of similar numeral letters (see at 2Ki 25:8). Evil-merodach: מרדך אויל, Εὔιαλ Μαρώδαχ or Εὐιαλμαρωδέκ (lxx); Ἰλλοαροόδαμος, possibly a copyist’s error for Ἰλμαροόδακος, in the <hi type="italic">Can. Ptol.</hi>, and in other forms also: see M. v. Nieb. <hi type="italic">Gesch. Ass.</hi> p. 42, and Ges. <hi type="italic">thes.</hi> p. 41; compounded from the name of the Babylonian god <hi type="italic">Merodach</hi> (see at 2Ki 20:12) and the prefix <hi type="italic">Evil</hi>, which has not yet been explained with certainty. He reigned two years, according to Berosus in Jos. <hi type="italic">c. Ap.</hi> i. 20, and the <hi type="italic">Can Ptol.</hi>; and according to the verdict of Berosus, προστὰς τῶν πραγμάτων ἀνόμως καὶ ἀσελγῶς; and was murdered by his brother-in-law Neriglissor. The statement in Jos. <hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> x. 11, 2, to the effect that he reigned eighteen years, and that of Alex. Polyh. in Euseb. <hi type="italic">Chr. arm.</hi> i. p. 45, that he reigned twelve years, are evidently false.
entries.2876127e883722024c27b6e5ee1e1c5baa83bd3a: 2Ki 25:28 “He spake kindly to him (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.12.6">Jer 12:6</reference>), and set his throne above the throne of the kings who were with him in Babel.” This is not to be understood literally, as signifying that he assigned him a loftier throne than the other kings (Hitzig, Thenius), but figuratively: <hi type="italic">loco honestiore eum habuit</hi> (Ros.). The “kings with him” were dethroned kings, who were kept at the court like Jehoiachin to add to its splendour, just as Cyrus kept the conquered Croesus by his side (Herod. i. 88).
entries.aac1a0e1824c0edff40749e0c74ec7cba9f7446b: 2Ki 25:29-30 “And he (Jehoiachin) changed his prison garments,” i.e., took them off and put other regal clothing on (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.41.42">Gen 41:42</reference>). “And ate continually before him all his life,” i.e., ate at the king’s table (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.7">2Sa 9:7</reference>). Moreover a daily ration of food was supplied to him by the king for the maintenance of his retainers, who formed his little court. The חיּיו כּל־ימי of 2Ki 25:30, upon which Thenius throws suspicion without any reason, refers to Jehoiachin like that in 2Ki 25:29; for the historian intended to show how Jehoiachin had fared from the day of his elevation to the end of his life. At the same time, we cannot infer from this with any certainty that Jehoiachin died before Evil-merodach; for the favour shown to him might be continued by Evil-merodach’s successor. We cannot make any safe conjecture as to the motives which induced Evil-merodach to pardon Jehoiachin and confer this distinction upon him. The higher ground of this joyful termination of his imprisonment lay in the gracious decree of God, that the seed of David, though severely chastised for its apostasy from the Lord, should not be utterly rejected (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14-2Sam.7.15">2Sa 7:14-15</reference>). At the same time, this event was also intended as a comforting sign to the whole of the captive people, that the Lord would one day put an end to their banishment, if they would acknowledge that it was a well-merited punishment for this sins that they had been driven away from before His face, and would turn again to the Lord their God with all their heart.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.25"/> <div eID="gen5515" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen5118" osisID="2Kgs" type="book"/>
